body.text: Technical Narrative Standards on Form T661 Part 2 and Classified Projects Protocol

Part 2 of Form T661 (Project Information) requires the claimant to establish, on a project-by-project basis, how the claimed work satisfies the Subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED. Under the CRA's Guide to Form T661 (T4088), claimants must adhere to three strict administrative rules when preparing Part 2. First, under the 20-Largest-Projects Filing Election, while a claimant must complete Part 2 for each project claimed for the taxation year and list all projects with their labour, materials, and contract expenditure breakdowns, the claimant may choose at the time of filing to submit Part 2 technical project descriptions for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value. However, the CRA explicitly reserves the authority to request Part 2 descriptions for some, or all, of the remaining projects at a later time, and failure to provide that information upon request results in the mandatory disallowance of the expenditures claimed for those projects as SR&ED expenditures.

Second, Section B of Part 2 enforces strict word limits on the responses to the technical narrative questions, which require the claimant to articulate the scientific or technological advancement sought, the scientific or technological uncertainties encountered, and the systematic investigation, experiments, or analyses formulated and executed to overcome those uncertainties. In Guide T4088, the CRA emphasizes that clear and concise descriptions that directly address the technical questions in the technical language and style of the qualified personnel who actually performed or supervised the work play a decisive role in enabling the CRA to establish reasonable confidence during initial desk screening and expedite processing without a full field audit, whereas vague, marketing-oriented, or unnecessarily lengthy descriptions increase the likelihood of an in-depth review. Third, under the National Security Protocol for Classified Projects, if a federal agency has designated any of a claimant's projects as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant must complete all parts of Form T661 on the return except that the project information requested in Section B of Part 2 for the classified projects must be prepared on a separate sheet and retained in the claimant's records rather than submitted with the tax return. The claimant must send a formal notification letter to the CRA's Technical Guidance Division / SR&ED Directorate at the address specified in Guide T4088 and include a copy of that letter with the income tax return filed alongside Form T661.
CRA Review Architecture and Audit Defence Best Practices

Upon receipt at the designated CRA tax centre (such as the Surrey Tax Centre in British Columbia or the Shawinigan-South National Verification and Collections Centre in Québec), an SR&ED claim undergoes an initial automated risk assessment and desk review. Where a claim is selected for technical and financial verification, the CRA assigns a coordinated dual-specialist review team comprising a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a domain scientist or engineer who evaluates whether the claimed projects satisfy the five Northwest Hydraulic eligibility criteria under Subsection 248(1) and whether claimed support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) is commensurate with the needs of the core experimental work—and a Financial Reviewer (FR)—a tax auditor who verifies general ledger reconciliations, T4/RL-1 payroll records, Specified Employee Form T1174 allocations, Subsection 78(4) unpaid wage adjustments, subcontractor taxable supplier status, and Subsection 127(18) government assistance grinds.

To withstand a coordinated CRA RTA and FR joint audit and substantiate claims under the modernized post-December 15, 2024 federal and provincial regimes, corporate claimants should embed four rigorous internal compliance controls into their ongoing engineering and accounting workflows. First, organizations should maintain contemporaneous project-level time tracking linked to specific technological uncertainties, ensuring that employee hours clearly distinguish between core experimental development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)), directly commensurate support work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)), and excluded commercial production, routine debugging, or post-deployment maintenance. Second, engineering and R&D teams must archive hypothesis-driven contemporaneous technical repositories—including dated design iterations, failed experimental test logs, laboratory notebooks, source-code commit histories, simulation outputs, and technical post-mortems generated as the work progressed—to satisfy the fifth Northwest Hydraulic judicial criterion without relying on retrospective reconstructions. Third, following the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment effective December 16, 2024 (and under Québec's post-March 25, 2025 CRIC regime), claimants acquiring depreciable R&D machinery and equipment must institute contemporaneous equipment operating-time logs to prove either that the asset was intended for and used ≥ 90% (all or substantially all) of its operating time in SR&ED, or that new equipment was used > 50% (primarily) of its operating time for SR&ED during the 12-month First Period and 24-month Second Period required for First Term and Second Term SUE claims. Fourth, legal and tax teams should review all subcontractor and research institute agreements prior to execution to verify that the contractor is a Canadian taxable supplier (or an eligible research institute for Ontario's 20% OBRITC or Québec's CRIC), that the contract statement of work explicitly mandates performance of the R&D within Canada (or within the specific province for provincial credits), and that the claimant retains the legal right to exploit the resulting intellectual property.
